title: Solving systems and polynomial equations with technology

moments.title: Using matrices for systems
moments.text: The video presents a matrix method for simultaneous equations. Matrix inverses are higher-level content; a calculator's simultaneous-equation solver also meets the SL technology requirement.

moments.title: Translate two orders into equations
moments.text: Let $c$ and $t$ be the prices of coffee and tea. The orders give $5c+3t=16.25$ and $2c+8t=15$.

moments.title: Write the system in matrix form
moments.text: The presenter arranges coefficients, unknowns and totals into $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$.

moments.title: From scalar algebra to matrices
moments.text: The presenter compares solving $3x=12$ with the matrix equation, then explains why a matrix inverse is used.

moments.title: Multiply by the inverse on the left
moments.text: Pre-multiplying both sides by $A^{-1}$ produces $A^{-1}A\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, provided $A$ is invertible.

moments.title: Apply the matrix method
moments.text: Use the coefficient matrix from the two orders and multiply its inverse by the column of totals.

moments.title: Evaluate the matrix expression
moments.text: The calculator gives $c=2.50$ and $t=1.25$; these values satisfy both original order equations.

moments.title: Extend the method
moments.text: The presenter explains that the same approach can be used with larger invertible coefficient matrices.

notes.title: SL and AHL methods
notes.text: This video uses matrix inverses, which are part of AHL matrix content. SL 1.8 requires technology to solve systems, but does not require this matrix method.
notes.write: A simultaneous-equation solver or graphical method can be used. State the values of the variables and check them in the original equations.

items.title: GDC Tips: Using nSolve to Solve Equations

moments.title: What a numerical solver does
moments.text: The video introduces a calculator tool for finding numerical solutions to equations.

moments.title: Set the population equal to the target
moments.text: The first model leads to $2000=50(1.24)^t$; the unknown is the time $t$.

moments.title: Enter the equation and unknown
moments.text: The presenter uses the TI-Nspire numerical solver to solve the population equation for $t$.

moments.title: Interpret the result
moments.text: The numerical solution is about $t=17.1$ to three significant figures; the answer represents the time at which the model reaches the stated population.

moments.title: A logarithmic example
moments.text: The second example models a sound level and asks for the intensity when the level is 124.

moments.title: Set up the logarithmic equation
moments.text: Substitute the target to obtain $124=10\log_{10}I+120$ and solve for the positive intensity $I$.

moments.title: Solve for intensity
moments.text: The calculator gives $I\approx2.51$ to three significant figures.

moments.title: Multiple solutions need care
moments.text: The video contrasts its single-solution examples with quadratic and cubic graphs where a chosen level may intersect more than once.

moments.title: Use a graph to investigate other solutions
moments.text: Graphing and intersection tools can help locate additional solutions within the relevant domain; check the window and any stated restrictions.

notes.title: Which root does a numerical solver return?
notes.text: The presenter says the solver always returns the left-hand solution. This is not a general guarantee: the returned solution can depend on the calculator, starting value, interval and algorithm.
notes.write: A numerical solve may return only one solution. Use the graph and appropriate intervals or starting values to investigate other solutions, then check them in the original equation.

notes.title: Different calculator
notes.text: The video demonstrates a TI-Nspire; your Casio fx-CG50 has different menus.
notes.write: Use the fx-CG50 equation or graph tools and follow the question's domain restrictions.

ican.text: I can enter and solve a system of linear equations in up to three variables using technology.
I can translate a contextual problem into equations and interpret the solution with units.
I can find all required real roots of a polynomial and distinguish roots from coordinates of intercepts.
I can use a graph, suitable search intervals and substitution to check numerical solutions.
I can state calculator results at an appropriate accuracy and respect a stated domain or context.

ku.text: A solution to a system makes every equation true at the same time. For two linear equations in two variables, it corresponds to the intersection of their graphs when one exists.
A root or zero of $f$ is an input $x$ such that $f(x)=0$. On a graph, a real root corresponds to the $x$-intercept $(x,0)$.
For $f(x)=g(x)$, solutions are the $x$-coordinates of intersections between the two graphs. Solving $f(x)-g(x)=0$ is an equivalent approach on the common domain.

A polynomial can have more than one real root. A numerical solver may return only one solution and can depend on a starting guess or search interval. A graph can guide the search but may hide roots outside its window or at a tangency.
A system of equations in a context requires consistent variable order, appropriate units and an interpretation. Substitute the values into each original equation to check.

Use technology for linear systems with up to three variables and polynomial equations. The syllabus guidance states that exam systems have a unique solution; outside that setting a system can have none or infinitely many.

misc.weak: The calculator gave $x=1$, so it is the only root.
misc.better: Investigate the graph and other intervals or use a polynomial solver to find all required real roots.
Solve $f(x)-g(x)=0$ or find the intersections of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$.

misc.weak: The solution of the system is $x=5$; no value for $y$ is needed.
misc.better: Report both coordinates, $x=5$ and $y=3$, when both variables are requested, and interpret them in context.

misc.weak: A graph that does not cross the axis in one window proves there are no roots.
misc.better: A root may lie outside the window or occur where the graph touches the axis. Use appropriate bounds and another method to check.

misc.weak: Enter coefficients in any order as long as every number is present.
misc.better: Keep the same variable order in every equation and include a zero coefficient for a missing variable.

terms.text: State all unknown values together, with units if applicable, and verify that they satisfy every equation.
Find all real $x$-values satisfying the equation on the specified domain; express intercepts as coordinates only when requested.
Relate each solution to the quantities and units in the problem and discard values that violate a stated context.

gdc.text: From the main menu, open Equation: [MENU] [XTT] (icon A). Wait for the menu to finish drawing.
For a two-variable system, choose [F1] SIMUL and [F1] for two unknowns. Enter the coefficients and constants in a consistent order, pressing [EXE] after each value; choose [F1] SOLVE.
For a quadratic, choose [F2] POLY and [F1] for degree 2. Enter the coefficients and choose [F1] SOLVE. Scroll to see the other root.
For a general numerical equation, choose [F3] SOLVER, enter the equation and press [EXE]. Set a suitable start value and bounds before [F6] SOLVE; check other intervals when needed.

worked.prompt: A school buys notebooks and pens. Two notebooks and three pens cost 19 dollars. Three notebooks and one pen cost 12 dollars. Let $x$ be the price of a notebook and $y$ the price of a pen, in dollars.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Write a system of equations and use technology to find $x$ and $y$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Check the solution in both equations.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Use technology to solve $x^3-2x^2-5x+6=0$ for all real values of $x$.
parts.a: The real roots are $x=-2,1,3$. A check is $x^3-2x^2-5x+6=(x+2)(x-1)(x-3)$.

kq.q: Why can a numerical solver find only one of several roots?
kq.model: A numerical search follows an algorithm from a starting value or within bounds. A different interval or starting value can lead to a different root, and no single initial search guarantees all roots.

kq.q: Why does an intersection solve both equations?
kq.model: At an intersection, the same point lies on both graphs. Its coordinates therefore satisfy both equations simultaneously.

kq.q: Why might a graph touch the x-axis without crossing it?
kq.model: A repeated real root can produce a tangency. Looking only for sign changes can miss such a root.

kq.q: Why should a contextual solution be checked even when the calculator returns it?
kq.model: The system may have been entered incorrectly, or a mathematically valid value may violate a stated domain or real-world restriction.
